source_title: James Bond's Most Divisive Movie Has Aged Better Than Fans Remember
source_excerpt:
Ask a group of people who their favorite James Bond actor is, and you will likely get a different answer. Some like Sean Connery's callous professionalism, others the louche, more comic Roger Moore era, and some prefer Daniel Craig's more grounded realism. While the debate over the best Bond is never-ending, audiences typically agree on the character's worst depiction. Poor George Lazenby. Following on from one of the most iconic portrayals of a film character was never going to be easy, but the start of On Her Majesty's Secret Service really makes a rod for its own back.
On Her Majesty's Secret Service kicks off with a fourth-wall-breaking nod to the camera, "This never happened to the other fella," and takes pains to reassure audiences this is the same 007, with a series of visual and audio cues to establish continuity. Producers were clearly terrified that audiences would reject Lazenby outright, but it meant that Lazenby wasn't really given the opportunity to deliver his own take. Until recently, On Her Majesty's Secret Service was regarded as one of the weakest Bond films, but the movie has undergone a critical re-evaluation, frequently appearing in at least the top five in any Bond rankings.
On Her Majesty's Secret Service Actually Had a Lot Going For It
No matter what you thought after the movie released in 1969, On Her Majesty's Secret Service 's sheer cinematic ambition is impressive. Peter Hunt , in his directing debut , brings character depth, a tender love story, and a real emphasis on the film's visuals, maybe due to the studio's tentative approach to Lazenby. The striking Alpine locations, dynamic action set-pieces, and more expressive visual style give On Her Majesty's Secret Service a distinct visual identity. Hunt employs a lot of stylized cinematography and shot composition, deploying extreme close-ups, psychedelic sequences, and an anamorphic widescreen aspect ratio to make the film stand out from its predecessors.
Additionally, the story itself is a lot more melancholy and considered than the more straightforward escapism of Connery's Bond films. The bittersweet ending, accompanied by Louis Armstrong's beautiful "We Have All The Time In The World," brings an emotional weight that the series wouldn't wholeheartedly attempt again until the Craig era. It's not for nothing that No Time to Die , the most overtly emotional film of Craig's tenure, would pay homage to the film's tragic ending by incorporating Armstrong's song into its score.
Another point in the film's favor is the Bond villain . Telly Savalas may not have the sinister appearance of Donald Pleasence's Ernst Stavro Blofeld, but he feels like a much more modern portrayal. He's charming, calculating, and, crucially, a physical match for Bond. Their scenes together carry a genuine sense of danger, especially their final fight. Ilse Steppat as Irma Bunt is another memorable henchwoman; her cold demeanor makes her an incredibly menacing figure, but Steppat's no-nonsense performance is bolstered by a dry sense of humor.
George Lazenby Had An Uphill Battle, And Still Did Pretty Well
Lazenby had no prior acting experience when he performed in On Her Majesty's Secret Service, and this shows at times, particularly when the script asks him to impersonate someone else. Still, he acquits himself pretty well. For much of the film, he needs to pretend to be someone else entirely, and the studio's decision to dub his dialogue in these scenes hampers him. For the most part, though, he is decent in the role and brings a physicality to Bond that suits the film's action sequences particularly well. Most importantly, he delivers the goods in the final scene, convincingly portraying Bond's grief and shock with a vulnerability that makes the ending so devastating.
Lazenby performed opposite perhaps the best " Bond girl " audiences had ever seen. Up to this point, the Bond heroines were largely treated as damsels in distress, disposable love interests, or women who existed solely to fall for Bond's charms. Tracy is a very different kind of character: she's impulsive, willful, and Bond's equal. Their relationship feels more substantial than another casual romance. For once, Bond has found a life beyond his work as a spy, which makes On Her Majesty's Secret Service 's conclusion all the more painful.

It's worth remembering that Lazenby wasn't simply fired after the critical response to On Her Majesty's Secret Service . He was, in fact, offered a contract for seven more films but chose to walk away, after his agent advised him that the Bond franchise would soon become outdated. It's tempting to wonder how he might have developed in the role with more experience. He might have become a much more celebrated Bond, or maybe not. Either way, judging his performance against Connery's six films was always going to be an uphill struggle.
Today, while On Her Majesty's Secret Service still feels like an outlier in the Bond series , it feels less like a failed attempt to replace Connery and more like an experiment in style and substance that the franchise wasn't quite ready for. Its distinct visuals, more emotionally raw Bond, and tragic ending anticipate more mature, modern elements that would become pivotal to Craig's tenure. Lazenby may never have had the chance to define the role across multiple films, but his one outing remains something utterly singular. The once-critically-panned Bond film has a unique feel, and its willingness to take risks has only become more impressive with time. Hopefully Denis Villeneuve explores some of this territory with his upcoming 007 film.
